concepts.topicTitle: Ecosystem Structure: Biotic and Abiotic Components
concepts.label: What an Ecosystem Is: Biotic and Abiotic Components
concepts.cardText: All organisms, such as plants, animals, microorganisms and human beings, as well as the physical surroundings interact with each other and maintain a balance in nature. All the interacting organisms in an area together with the non-living constituents of the environment form an ecosystem. An ecosystem consists of biotic components, the living organisms, and abiotic components, physical factors like temperature, rainfall, wind, soil and minerals. A garden, with grasses, trees, flowering plants, frogs, insects and birds whose growth and activities are affected by the abiotic factors, is an ecosystem. Forests, ponds and lakes are natural ecosystems, while gardens and crop-fields are human-made (artificial) ecosystems. An aquarium is also a human-made ecosystem that can become self-sustaining if a few aquatic plants and animals are added.

concepts.topicTitle: Ecosystem Structure: Biotic and Abiotic Components
concepts.label: Producers, Consumers and Decomposers
concepts.cardText: Organisms can be grouped as producers, consumers and decomposers according to how they obtain their sustenance. Green plants and certain bacteria that make organic compounds like sugar and starch from inorganic substances using the radiant energy of the Sun in the presence of chlorophyll, by photosynthesis, are the producers. Organisms that consume the food produced, directly from producers or indirectly by feeding on other consumers, are the consumers: herbivores, carnivores, omnivores and parasites. Microorganisms, bacteria and fungi, break down the dead remains and waste products of organisms: they are the decomposers. They break down complex organic substances into simple inorganic substances that go into the soil and are used up once more by plants.

concepts.topicTitle: Trophic Levels, Food Chains and Unidirectional Energy Flow
concepts.label: Food Chains and Trophic Levels
concepts.cardText: A series of organisms feeding on one another, taking part at various biotic levels, forms a food chain. Each step or level of the food chain forms a trophic level. The autotrophs, or producers, are at the first trophic level, fixing solar energy and making it available to the heterotrophs, or consumers. The herbivores, or primary consumers, come at the second level, small carnivores or secondary consumers at the third, and larger carnivores or tertiary consumers form the fourth trophic level. The interactions among components of the environment involve a flow of energy from one component to another: autotrophs capture the energy in sunlight and convert it into chemical energy that supports all the activities of the living world, passing from autotrophs to heterotrophs and decomposers.

concepts.topicTitle: Trophic Levels, Food Chains and Unidirectional Energy Flow
concepts.label: Flow of Energy: The 10 Per Cent Law and Why Food Chains Are Short
concepts.cardText: Autotrophs capture the energy of sunlight and convert it into chemical energy that supports all activities of the living world; from them the energy goes to heterotrophs and decomposers. When one form of energy changes to another, some energy is lost to the environment in forms that cannot be used again. Green plants in a terrestrial ecosystem capture about 1% of the energy of sunlight falling on their leaves. When plants are eaten by primary consumers, a great deal of energy is lost as heat, some goes into digestion and doing work, and the rest goes to growth and reproduction. An average of 10% of the food eaten is turned into the consumer's own body and made available to the next level. Because so little energy reaches the next level, food chains generally have only three or four steps. The flow of energy is unidirectional: it does not revert to the solar input or back to the previous level, and the energy available at each trophic level gets diminished progressively.

concepts.label: Food Webs
concepts.cardText: The length and complexity of food chains vary greatly. Each organism is generally eaten by two or more other kinds of organisms, which in turn are eaten by several other organisms. So, instead of a straight line food chain, the relationship can be shown as a series of branching lines called a food web. A food web consists of many food chains linked together. There are generally a greater number of individuals at the lower trophic levels of an ecosystem, with the greatest number being of the producers.

concepts.label: Biological Magnification
concepts.cardText: Some harmful chemicals unknowingly enter our bodies through the food chain. Pesticides and other chemicals used to protect crops from diseases and pests are washed down into the soil or into water bodies. From the soil they are absorbed by plants along with water and minerals, and from the water bodies they are taken up by aquatic plants and animals, so they enter the food chain. As these chemicals are not degradable, they get accumulated progressively at each trophic level. Because human beings occupy the top level in any food chain, the maximum concentration of these chemicals accumulates in our bodies. This phenomenon is known as biological magnification. This is why food grains such as wheat and rice, vegetables, fruits and even meat contain varying amounts of pesticide residues, which cannot always be removed by washing.

concepts.topicTitle: Ozone Layer Depletion and the Environmental Impact of Waste
concepts.label: The Ozone Layer and How It Is Depleted
concepts.cardText: Ozone (O3) is a molecule formed by three atoms of oxygen. While O2, which we normally call oxygen, is essential for all aerobic forms of life, ozone is a deadly poison. However, at the higher levels of the atmosphere, ozone performs an essential function: it shields the surface of the earth from the Sun's ultraviolet (UV) radiation, which is highly damaging to organisms and is known to cause skin cancer in humans. Ozone at the higher levels is a product of UV radiation acting on oxygen: higher energy UV splits some oxygen molecules into free oxygen atoms, which combine with molecular oxygen to form ozone. The amount of ozone began to drop sharply in the 1980s, linked to synthetic chemicals like chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) used as refrigerants and in fire extinguishers. In 1987 UNEP forged an agreement to freeze CFC production at 1986 levels, and it is now mandatory for manufacturers worldwide to make CFC-free refrigerators.

concepts.label: Biodegradable and Non-biodegradable Waste
concepts.cardText: Enzymes are specific in their action: specific enzymes are needed to break down a particular substance, which is why we get no energy from eating coal. Because of this, many human-made materials like plastics are not broken down by the action of bacteria or other saprophytes; they are acted on by physical processes like heat and pressure, but under ambient conditions persist for a long time. Substances that are broken down by biological processes are biodegradable; those that are not are non-biodegradable. Non-biodegradable substances may be inert and simply persist in the environment for a long time, or may harm members of the ecosystem. Improvements in life-style have resulted in greater amounts of waste, more things we use have become disposable, and changes in packaging have made much of our waste non-biodegradable. Disposal of the waste we generate is causing serious environmental problems.
